units.name: request-response-model
units.role: Defines what an HTTP request and response *are* as data, without performing network I/O itself.
units.description: This is the core vocabulary of the library: it defines the shape of an HTTP request before it is sent (Request), the exact wire-ready version of that request (PreparedRequest), and the object that represents a server's reply (Response), including its status code, headers, cookies, and body. It also provides everyday conveniences people use on a response, like reading it as text, parsing it as JSON, iterating over it in chunks, following pagination links, and raising an error for bad status codes. It does not open network connections itself; it hands that job to the transport-adapter unit and only unpacks or repackages the data that unit gives back.

entrypoints.name: Request
entrypoints.plain: The user-facing object for describing an HTTP request (method, url, headers, data, etc.) before it's prepared for sending.

entrypoints.name: Request.prepare
entrypoints.plain: Turns a user-built Request into a fully-formed PreparedRequest ready to be sent.

entrypoints.name: PreparedRequest
entrypoints.plain: The exact-bytes version of a request that Session and adapters actually transmit.

entrypoints.name: PreparedRequest.prepare
entrypoints.signature: def prepare(self, method=None, url=None, headers=None, files=None, data=None, params=None, auth=None, cookies=None, hooks=None, json=None) -> None

entrypoints.name: PreparedRequest.prepare_cookies

entrypoints.name: PreparedRequest.prepare_auth
entrypoints.plain: Runs an auth handler over the request; called directly by Session when auth changes after a redirect.

entrypoints.name: Response
entrypoints.plain: The object returned to callers describing what the server sent back: status, headers, cookies, body.

entrypoints.name: Response.iter_content
entrypoints.plain: Lets a caller read the response body piece by piece instead of all at once.

entrypoints.signature: def iter_lines(self, chunk_size=ITER_CHUNK_SIZE, decode_unicode=False, delimiter=None) -> Iterator[str|bytes]

entrypoints.plain: The full response body as raw bytes.

entrypoints.name: Response.text

entrypoints.name: Response.json
entrypoints.plain: Parses the response body as JSON.

entrypoints.name: Response.links
entrypoints.plain: Parsed pagination/relation links from the response's Link header.

entrypoints.name: Response.raise_for_status
entrypoints.plain: Raises an error if the response represents an HTTP client or server error.

entrypoints.name: Response.close
entrypoints.plain: Releases the underlying network connection back to the pool; called by Session and by users via `with` blocks.

entrypoints.name: Response.ok
entrypoints.plain: True if the response did not represent an error status.

entrypoints.name: REDIRECT_STATI
entrypoints.plain: The set of status codes considered automatic redirects; used by the session unit's redirect-following logic.

entrypoints.name: DEFAULT_REDIRECT_LIMIT
entrypoints.plain: Default cap on redirects a Session will follow.

effects.description: Response.iter_content()/iter_lines() read bytes off self.raw (a live urllib3 HTTPResponse handed to it by the transport-adapter unit) via self.raw.stream(...)/self.raw.read(chunk_size) (models.py:939, 951); Response.close() calls self.raw.close()/release_conn() (models.py:1173-1184) to release the connection.
Response.elapsed is a datetime.timedelta recorded around the request (models.py:806, 748).

units.name: session
units.role: Builds, sends, and follows redirects for HTTP requests, either one-off (module-level functions) or across many calls via a persistent Session that remembers cookies, auth, headers, and connections.
units.description: This is the part of the library that actually lets you 'make a web request.' It offers two ways to do that: quick one-off helpers like requests.get(url) for when you just want a single answer from a website, and a reusable Session object for when you want to talk to the same website repeatedly and have it remember things like login cookies, custom headers, and open connections between calls (which is faster and handles redirects and shared authentication correctly). The one-off helpers are a thin convenience layer that creates a temporary Session, uses it once, and discards it, so they are grouped with Session rather than split into their own unit.

units.name: transport-adapter
units.role: Wraps urllib3 connection pooling to open sockets, verify TLS, handle proxies, and turn raw urllib3 responses into requests.Response objects.
units.description: This is the part of the library that actually reaches out onto the network. When a request is ready to be sent, this code picks (or opens) a connection to the right server, optionally through a proxy, checks that the site's security certificate is valid, sends the request bytes, and converts whatever comes back into the Response object the rest of the library and end users work with. It does not decide whether to follow redirects or apply cookies across a session — it only handles the low-level plumbing of one network exchange.

entrypoints.name: BaseAdapter

entrypoints.name: HTTPAdapter

units.name: auth
units.role: Implements HTTP authentication schemes (Basic, Proxy-Basic, Digest) that requests can attach to outgoing requests and use to respond to 401 challenges.
units.description: This unit knows how to prove a user's identity to a web server using the two authentication styles built into the HTTP protocol: Basic Auth, which just encodes a username and password, and Digest Auth, which involves a back-and-forth challenge from the server that this code answers with a cryptographic response. It does not open any network connections itself; it only computes headers and reacts to responses that the networking code hands it.

entrypoints.name: AuthBase
entrypoints.plain: Base interface for auth handlers: called with the outgoing request so it can attach credentials.

entrypoints.name: HTTPBasicAuth
entrypoints.plain: Attaches a Basic Authorization header to a request; used by models.py when a (user, pass) tuple is passed as auth.

entrypoints.name: HTTPProxyAuth

entrypoints.name: HTTPDigestAuth
entrypoints.plain: Registers response hooks so digest auth can react to a server's 401 challenge and resend the request with a computed digest header.

entrypoints.name: _basic_auth_str
entrypoints.signature: def _basic_auth_str(username: bytes | str, password: bytes | str) -> str
entrypoints.plain: Builds the raw 'Basic <base64>' string; called directly by the session and transport-adapter units to build proxy auth headers without a full HTTPBasicAuth object.

effects.description: HTTPDigestAuth.build_digest_header calls time.ctime() (auth.py:234) to seed the client nonce with the current time.
HTTPDigestAuth.build_digest_header calls os.urandom(8) (auth.py:235) for entropy in the client nonce, hashed together with the time via SHA-1.

HTTPDigestAuth.handle_401 calls r.connection.send(prep, **kwargs) (auth.py:312) to resend the request with the computed digest header, and reads/closes the prior response to drain its connection; the actual socket I/O is performed by the connection object handed to it by the transport-adapter unit, not opened here.

units.name: cookies
units.role: Adapts Python's stdlib http.cookiejar so the rest of requests can store, merge, and read cookies via a dict-like jar or plain dict.
units.description: This is the translation layer between the plain HTTP cookies that servers send and receive, and Python's built-in cookie-jar machinery. It lets the rest of the library treat cookies almost like a simple dictionary (look one up by name, set one, merge two collections together) while staying fully compatible with the more rigorous, policy-aware cookie jar Python ships with. It does not decide what a cookie means to a request; it just gives everyone else a convenient, consistent way to carry cookies around.

units.name: exceptions
units.role: Defines the complete hierarchy of errors and warnings that the requests library can raise or emit.
units.description: This file lists every kind of problem that can happen when the library tries to make a web request or handle its response — things like a bad URL, a connection failure, a timeout, too many redirects, or a response that isn't valid JSON. It organizes these problems into a family tree so that code elsewhere in the library, and programs that use the library, can catch a broad category of error or a very specific one. It does not perform any actions itself; it only names and describes the ways things can go wrong.

units.name: structures
units.role: Provides simple reusable container types (a case-insensitive dict and a friendly-lookup dict) plus the ready-made HTTP status-code name table built from them.
units.description: This unit contains small, general-purpose data containers that other parts of the library use to organize information, rather than logic about making requests itself. One container is a dictionary that ignores upper/lower case differences in its keys, used to store HTTP headers so 'Content-Type' and 'content-type' are treated as the same header. The other is a dictionary that returns a friendly None instead of crashing when you look up a name it doesn't recognize; it is used to build a single ready-made table, `codes`, which lets other code look up HTTP status codes by friendly name (like codes.ok for 200) instead of memorizing numbers. None of this code talks to the network, disk, or clock.

entrypoints.name: CaseInsensitiveDict
entrypoints.plain: A dictionary type used to store HTTP headers so key lookups ignore case.

entrypoints.name: LookupDict
entrypoints.plain: A dictionary type that returns None instead of raising on unknown keys; used to build the codes table.

entrypoints.name: codes

effects.description: Heuristic-only: status_codes.py's module docstring contains the literal example line '>>> import requests' (status_codes.py:8), which the text-pattern effect detector matches as a 'network' signal. This is a documentation example, not executable code — the module itself is pure data (a LookupDict of status codes) with no I/O of any kind.

units.name: hooks
units.role: Small event-dispatch mechanism for running user-registered callbacks against a Response.
units.description: This unit is a tiny, general-purpose plugin mechanism. It lets someone using the library register a custom function that automatically runs whenever a network response comes back, so they can inspect or modify that response without changing the library's own code. It does not perform any networking itself; it just keeps track of registered functions and calls them at the right moment when asked to by other parts of the library.

entrypoints.name: default_hooks
entrypoints.plain: Creates an empty hook table (one empty list per known event, currently just 'response').

entrypoints.name: dispatch_hook
entrypoints.signature: def dispatch_hook(key: str, hooks, hook_data: Response, **kwargs) -> Response
entrypoints.plain: Runs all registered callbacks for a given event against a piece of data, letting each callback optionally replace it.

units.name: http-utils
units.role: Stateless helper functions for proxy resolution, encoding detection, header parsing, request-body sizing, and CA bundle location.
units.description: This is a toolbox of small, reusable helper functions that other parts of the library call on to do fiddly technical chores: deciding which proxy server should be used for a given web address by checking environment variables and the user's .netrc credentials file, guessing what text encoding a server's response is written in, figuring out how big a request body is so the correct Content-Length header can be sent, parsing and building the small bits of syntax used inside HTTP header values, and finding the bundled file of trusted security certificates used to verify HTTPS connections. None of these functions represent what a web request means in a business sense; they are plumbing the rest of the library leans on to talk correctly to the network and the operating system.

units.name: foundation
units.role: Version-agnostic scaffolding (stdlib/urllib3 compatibility shims, tiny string/type helpers, version metadata, and legacy import aliasing) that every other unit imports but which contains no HTTP behavior itself.
units.description: This is the plumbing underneath the library rather than a feature of it. It gives the rest of the code stable, version-independent names to import so it doesn't matter whether the user has an old or new Python, or an old or new urllib3, or chardet vs charset_normalizer installed. It also provides a couple of tiny helper functions for normalizing strings and header values, a few internal type definitions used for static type-checking, the library's version number, and a compatibility trick so old code written against requests.packages.urllib3 still works. None of these files know or care about HTTP requests, cookies, or sessions.

effects.description: compat.py:102 does `from urllib.request import (getproxies, getproxies_environment, parse_http_list, proxy_bypass, proxy_bypass_environment)` — matched by the text-pattern effect detector on the literal substring 'urllib.request'. In practice only proxy-configuration helpers are used from that module (no urlopen/connection calls); no sockets are opened by this file.

compat.py inspects the running environment at import time: reads sys.version_info, parses urllib3's version string to set is_urllib3_1, and tries importing chardet, then charset_normalizer, then simplejson (falling back to json), swallowing ImportError. This is environment/feature detection, not classic I/O, but it does make behavior depend on what's installed.

packages.py mutates global interpreter state: it writes entries into sys.modules (e.g. sys.modules['requests.packages.urllib3']) so that `import requests.packages.urllib3` resolves to the real urllib3 module.

units.name: diagnostics
units.role: Collects and prints Python/OS/SSL/dependency version info for bug reports.
units.description: This is a small self-help tool bundled with the requests library. When someone hits a bug and needs to file a report, they can run one command and it prints a tidy summary of their computer's setup: which Python they are using, which operating system, which version of the secure-connection software is installed, and which versions of requests' optional helper libraries are present. This saves back-and-forth between bug reporters and maintainers.

entrypoints.name: main

effects.description: Introspects installed Python/OS/SSL/optional-dependency (idna, urllib3, chardet, charset_normalizer, cryptography, pyOpenSSL) versions for bug reports; no network or filesystem writes.

units.name: package-init
units.role: The import-time entry point for the requests package: validates dependency versions, patches SSL/SNI support when needed, silences noisy warnings, sets up logging, and assembles the public requests.* namespace.
units.description: This is the file that runs the moment someone types `import requests`. It doesn't implement HTTP logic itself; instead it does housekeeping: it checks that the versions of helper libraries installed alongside requests are compatible and warns the user if not, it works around old Python builds that lack secure-connection (SNI) support by patching in an alternative SSL backend, it tells Python to ignore a specific noisy warning from urllib3 and to show a warning about file modes by default, and it quiets an unrelated logging warning. It then re-exports the names (like Session, Response, get, post, and codes) that are actually built in other units, so users can call requests.get(...) instead of digging into submodules.

entrypoints.name: check_compatibility
entrypoints.plain: Public function (requests.check_compatibility) that asserts installed urllib3/chardet/charset_normalizer versions fall within supported ranges; run internally at import time.

effects.description: Heuristic-only: __init__.py's module docstring contains the literal example line '>>> import requests' (__init__.py:13), which the text-pattern effect detector matches as a 'network' signal. This is a documentation example, not executable code.

Conditionally monkey-patches urllib3's SSL backend at import time via urllib3.contrib.pyopenssl.inject_into_urllib3() when the standard library's ssl module lacks SNI support; configures global warnings filters (silencing urllib3's DependencyWarning, showing FileModeWarning by default) and attaches a logging NullHandler to the 'requests' logger.

violations_observed.note: HTTPDigestAuth.handle_401 calls r.connection.send(prep, **kwargs) directly on whatever connection object the response carries, rather than going through a listed transport-adapter entrypoint (adapters.HTTPAdapter.send is a Session-facing method, not something auth.py formally depends on). This is a real but narrow coupling: auth reaches into a live connection handed to it by the response rather than asking the session to resend.
